title: A heart of flesh (Ezekiel 36:26)
hookLine: I will take out the heart of stone

cards: Stone doesn't feel anything. That's what makes it good for walls. A sibling, an old friend, a parent, a coworker: someone hurts a person enough times, and something in that person goes hard.
The name pops up on a phone, and there's nothing, or worse, a cold click. It works like protection, and sometimes it is. But walls spread: harder with one person, then a little harder with everyone.
Ezekiel had watched a whole people grow hard: toward God, toward the poor, toward the truth. And he heard a promise about the heart.

teach.h: A NEW HEART WILL I GIVE YOU.
teach.b: In the King James Bible, God says through Ezekiel: "A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh."
In the Hebrew Bible, the heart, lev, isn't mainly where you feel.

teach.h: LEV: WHERE YOU THINK AND CHOOSE.
teach.b: It's often where people think, decide and choose: the whole inner self. So a heart of stone isn't just sadness. It's a self that can't be moved, taught or reached.
A heart of flesh is alive again, soft enough to feel, to change, to care. The trade isn't weak for strong. It's stone for flesh.

teach.h: ONLY FLESH CAN BE HURT, OR LOVE.
teach.b: Flesh can be hurt, and that's the point: only something that can be hurt can also love. Now look back to chapter eighteen.

teach.h: MAKE IT, OR RECEIVE IT? BOTH.
teach.b: There Ezekiel tells the people: make you a new heart and a new spirit. Make it yourselves. Here, God says: I will give it.
So which is it? The book holds both.
Some readers put it this way: the new heart is something you're called to reach for, and something you can only receive.
Christians often connect this verse to the work of the Holy Spirit; Jewish readers hear God's promise to renew Israel after exile. Both hear the same image: stone taken out, flesh given back.

how: Christians often pray Ezekiel 36:26 when asking God to change them, and it is read at the Easter Vigil, at confirmations and at services of renewal; it appears in many hymns and worship songs about the Spirit.

o: the breath of life that God blows into a body
a feeling of warmth or affection for someone
the inner self, where you think, decide and choose

games.q: what's inside the promise — tap the pairs.
p: where you think, decide and choose
a new heart will I give you

s: in Hebrew, the heart is mainly where feelings live
lev is the whole inner self: where you think, decide and choose.
Ezekiel tells people to make a new heart, and also says God will give one
chapter eighteen says make you a new heart; chapter thirty-six says I will give you one.
the promise swaps a weak heart for a stronger, harder one
it swaps stone for flesh: something soft enough to be hurt, and to love.

games.q: you've noticed your heart has gone hard. where does the new heart come from, according to Ezekiel?
o: you have to make it yourself, by effort.
both: you're told to make one, and God promises to give one.
it never changes once it's hard.
games.why: Ezekiel 18:31 says make you a new heart; 36:26 says a new heart also will I give you. the book holds both.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've gone hard toward; not the one who hurt you most, someone smaller.

Notice the stone, the tight chest, the ready list of what they did, and set the list down for a minute while you see one ordinary, human thing about them: they get tired, they were a child once, someone they love is sick.
Let your chest loosen by one degree, and if you pray, ask for a heart of flesh.

wordCard.voice: Lev. The Hebrew word for heart, the whole inner self: where you think, decide and choose, not only where you feel.

orig.note: Hebrew: a heart of flesh. lev means the whole inner self.

carryVoice: Your line: loosen by one degree. Stone can't love; flesh can. Day four hundred seventy-nine, done.
